title: Walnut vs Consensus vs Storylane Demo Suite (2026)
summary: Walnut vs Consensus vs Storylane Demo Suite compared: interactive demos vs video demos, real pricing, setup time, and analytics, so you pick the right demo platform fast.
body_markdown:
The Walnut vs Consensus decision looks like a feature bake-off, but it is really one question: do your buyers need interactive, click-through demos they explore themselves, or async video they can forward to a committee? Answer that, and price, setup time, and analytics all fall into place.


I run marketing at Storylane, so I have a horse in this race, and I will flag exactly where that bias sits. Everywhere else I keep it straight, because a comparison that pretends to be neutral and then pivots into a pitch helps nobody.


> **Definition:** Demo automation software lets teams build and share product demos, interactive walkthroughs or recorded video, that prospects can experience without a live rep on every call.


## Walnut vs Consensus at a glance


Here is the short version. Consensus is the older, video-first platform built around distributing demos to buying committees, while Walnut is the interactive click-through builder that captures your product as a guided tour. Neither is objectively better: they optimize for different buying motions, and the wrong fit costs you either engagement or reach.


Dimension Walnut Consensus


Founded 2020 2013


Category Interactive click-through demos Async video demos, plus interactive tours


Best for Self-serve product exploration Distributing demos to buying committees


G2 rating ~4.5 (150+ reviews) ~4.7 (1,700+ reviews; per G2, verify current count at g2.com)


Free trial Limited / demo-gated Demo-gated


Public flat pricing No No


G2 ratings and review counts are current as of this year (G2, 2026). Treat the "best for" column as a starting hypothesis, not a verdict: the rest of this guide tests it against pricing, setup time, and analytics.


Two things stand out even here. Consensus has a much deeper review base and a slightly higher satisfaction score, reflecting its head start, while Walnut is younger and more interactive by design, so its numbers read as a challenger's. Do not let review volume decide the purchase: it rewards age and reach more than fit for your specific motion.


## The core difference in Walnut vs Consensus: interactive vs video demos


This is the axis that decides everything else, and most comparison pages skip past it. Consensus is fundamentally about async, buyer-driven video: a prospect opens a demo, self-selects what matters to them, and forwards it to colleagues while the platform tracks who watched what. Walnut is fundamentally about interactive tours: a clickable capture of your product that a buyer navigates like the real thing.


The format changes the buyer's experience, not just yours. One marketing leader described why the seamlessness matters when video and clicks blend well versus badly.


> "The way \[Consensus\] integrated their video was click through, click through ... whereas like a video just kind of takes you out of it." - Marketing leader at a communication software company


If your motion is committee-based and reach-driven, video that forwards well wins. If your motion is self-serve and hands-on, interactive exploration wins. Storylane's own take on where recorded video still earns its place is in this breakdown of[video-based product demos](https://www.storylane.io/blog/saas-product-demo-and-explainer-videos) .


## What is Walnut?


Walnut is a no-code interactive demo platform, founded in 2020 (Crunchbase, 2025), built for solutions and marketing teams that want prospects to click through a realistic product experience. It captures screens or HTML from your product and stitches them into guided, personalizable tours, increasingly with AI assistance on the build side.


Where Walnut is strong:


- No-code builder with product capture, so non-engineers can assemble a tour.
- AI-assisted demo creation and personalization at scale across accounts.
- Click-level analytics on how prospects move through a tour.


Where buyers push back:


- Captured tours can feel screengrab-based, and specific interactivity often needs repeated manual re-captures.
- Its embedded video snippets do not always blend into the interactive flow, as one buyer put it bluntly.


> "Right now with Walnut, they also have a video snippet ... it doesn't seamlessly go, like you feel like you pop out of the demo." - Director of product marketing at a software company


Walnut's G2 rating (~4.5) sits below the category's top scorers, which is worth weighing if peer validation matters to you.


## What is Consensus?


Consensus is the category's elder statesman, founded in 2013 (Crunchbase, 2025), and it built its reputation on intelligent demo video. Consensus describes its core as DemoBoards and BuyerBoard stakeholder tracking, Demolytics engagement analytics, and Choose-Your-Own-Journey branching that lets a prospect self-select the story that fits their role.


The nuance most pages miss is recent. Consensus acquired Reachsuite in 2024 (PR Newswire, 2024) to add HTML and interactive tours on top of its video foundation, so calling it "video only" is now out of date. That introduces a real question: two experiences that must feel like one, or they create extra work for the team maintaining them.


Consensus's strengths are reach and intelligence at the committee level: it shines when a demo must travel across a buying group and report back who engaged and for how long. If Consensus is on your shortlist, weigh[other Consensus alternatives](https://www.storylane.io/blog/consensus-alternatives) too, so you choose it on merit rather than defaulting to the incumbent because it is the older name.


## Feature-by-feature comparison


Both platforms cover the table stakes: demo creation, personalization, analytics, and CRM integration. The differences are in emphasis, and emphasis is what you are actually buying. The rows below reflect each vendor's own publicly described capabilities.


Capability Walnut Consensus


Demo creation Product capture, interactive tours Recorded video, plus interactive tours (post-Reachsuite)


Personalization Tour-level, at scale Branching journeys per stakeholder


Analytics Click and engagement per tour Demolytics plus buyer-committee tracking


Integrations Salesforce, HubSpot Salesforce, HubSpot, native Gong edge


AI Build assistance and translation AI Content Studio


Localization Multi-language support Available


Read the table by your priority, not feature count. Walnut leans into interactive build depth and language coverage; Consensus leans into committee analytics and its native Gong integration. Both integrate with Salesforce and HubSpot, so CRM sync is table stakes rather than a differentiator.


The AI story differs on each side. Walnut applies AI to build and translation while Consensus's AI Content Studio leans toward generating and packaging demo content for distribution, so weigh AI as an accelerant, not a reason to buy. One buyer summed up why granular analytics is often the deciding line.


> "I want to make sure that we can determine when someone's clicked on something, which one is getting the most clicks ... and how long were they in it?" - Cybersecurity lead at a cybersecurity company


## Pricing compared


Start with the honest part: neither Walnut nor Consensus publishes flat public rates, and every "official price" you find online is an entry point or an estimate. Public entry data on G2 shows Consensus starting around $600 per month and Walnut around $750 per year for a small editor-seat pack (G2, 2026). Those are floors for the smallest configuration, not what a mid-market or enterprise team actually pays.


Real cost is driven by seats, demo volume, and add-ons, and it is negotiated. Ask each vendor for pricing at your seat count and a two-year view including onboarding, because that is where the gap between list and reality appears.


Budget, not features, is often the true gatekeeper. As one buyer put it, the choice usually collapses to a single funded platform.


> "I don't think that we are going to get two platforms. So either they get convinced that the one offer by consensus is the one to go ... or they will be just going to one platform." - Strategic marketing manager at a communications company


## Implementation time and time-to-value


Setup effort tracks the format difference directly, and it is a real deciding factor even though most comparison pages skip it. Interactive click-capture tools tend to reach a first usable demo quickly, because a team can record the product and assemble a tour without heavy production. Async video libraries with stakeholder tracking usually take longer, because you are producing video and configuring committee routing before the first buyer sees anything.


If you need speed to value, sequence your rollout like this:


1. Capture or record one high-priority demo for your best-known use case.
2. Wire the analytics and CRM sync so you can prove engagement to your team.
3. Template it, then hand the pattern to reps or marketing to scale.


The trap to avoid is boiling the ocean: teams that try to build twenty demos before launch stall. One buyer's mandate was refreshingly narrow, and that focus is why it moved.


> "I've been tasked with building a self guided demo experience for a big conference we're having in a month or so." - Head of product marketing at a software company


## Which converts better in Walnut vs Consensus? Demo engagement benchmarks


Be skeptical of any single conversion number here. Vendor-reported lifts, on both sides, are self-reported and unbenchmarked, so I will not repeat them as fact. What I trust more is buyer behavior: prospects disengage the instant a demo feels like it broke or "popped out" of the experience.


Signal Interactive tours Async video


Best funnel moment Mid-funnel hands-on validation Early reach and committee sharing


Engagement style Active clicking and exploration Passive watching, forwardable


Failure mode Screengrab feel, broken interactivity Video that pulls the buyer out


Interactive tends to win when buyers want to touch the product themselves; video tends to win when the job is broadcasting a consistent story to people you will never get on a call. The failure modes matter as much as the wins: a broken interactive tour and a video that pulls the buyer out both kill momentum instantly.


Match the format to the funnel moment rather than chasing one universal conversion number. Early, wide committee reach favors async video; mid-funnel, hands-on validation favors interactive tours. Both beat the live-demo bottleneck buyers keep describing, which is also why the format matters when[handling inbound demo requests](https://www.storylane.io/blog/demo-requests) that would otherwise go cold.


## Best for: pick by team type and buying motion


The cleanest way to choose is to map the tool to your motion, not your feature wishlist. Use this decision list as a starting point:


- **By stage:** Seed to Series A teams that live on self-serve exploration lean interactive; later-stage teams selling to large committees get more from async video reach.
- **By owner:** SE and presales leaders usually want interactive fidelity; RevOps wants clean CRM and analytics signal; PMM wants scalable, on-message distribution.
- **By buying motion:** Product-led and hands-on evaluations favor Walnut-style tours; sales-led, multi-stakeholder deals favor Consensus-style video distribution.


Decision tree, start here: if your buyers must experience the product to believe it, choose interactive. If your bottleneck is reaching people who will never join a call, choose async video, and if it is both, weight by whichever costs you more deals today. Whatever you pick, make sure it earns its slot in[your sales tech stack](https://www.storylane.io/blog/tools-to-build-the-best-sales-tech-stack) rather than duplicating a tool you already own.

The reason we exist is the pain buyers keep naming: authenticity they trust in front of a customer, and self-serve validation without a rep on the call.


> "We need to be able to show whatever we're producing consistently ... it looks and feels like the real thing. Enough to that where we could pass it out as a version." - Marketing leader at a communication software company

## Buyer's decision checklist and scorecard


No top-10 page hands you a reusable scorecard, so here is one. Score each tool 1 to 5 on the criteria that actually move a demo-automation decision, weight them for your team, and total the columns.


Criterion Weight Walnut Consensus


Interactivity and product fidelity High Score Score


Video and committee distribution High Score Score


Analytics granularity High Score Score


Build speed and time-to-value Medium Score Score


CRM and Gong integration Medium Score Score


Total cost at your seat count High Score Score


The weighting is the point: an SE-led team should weight fidelity and build speed heavily, while a committee-selling team should weight distribution and analytics. Fill the score cells during your own trials rather than trusting a vendor's grid, because the numbers only mean something when they reflect your product and your buyers.


Run the same rubric across both platforms in parallel, using one real use case, so you are comparing like with like. Buyers who trial concurrently and score against fixed criteria make faster, more defensible decisions than teams that judge on demos and gut feel. If you want a wider field to score against, this list[comparing demo automation tools](https://www.storylane.io/blog/tourial-alternatives) gives you more rows to run through the same rubric.


## Migration and "can I run both?" reality check


Almost nobody addresses this honestly, so let me. Most teams will not fund two demo platforms, which means the realistic question is not "run both" but "which one, and what does switching cost."


- **What migrates:** demo content usually rebuilds rather than ports, since capture formats differ; your CRM mappings, dashboards, and templates are the real switching cost.
- **When running both makes sense:** rarely, and only when one tool owns async committee video and the other owns interactive self-serve, with separate use cases and budget.
- **When it does not:** when the two overlap on the same job, you pay twice for one outcome and split your analytics.


If budget forces one platform, decide on the format axis first, then migrate deliberately: rebuild your top demo natively, validate engagement, and retire the old tool once the new one proves out. In the end, the Walnut vs Consensus choice comes back to the question at the top: interactive exploration or async video reach, and which your buyers actually need to say yes.

## Frequently asked questions


### Which is more expensive, Walnut or Consensus?


Neither publishes flat public pricing, so a blanket answer is misleading. Public entry points on G2 show Consensus starting around $600 per month and Walnut around $750 per year for a small seat pack (G2, 2026). Real cost depends on seats and add-ons, so get quotes at your configuration.


### Which is faster to implement?


Interactive click-capture tools like Walnut generally reach a first usable demo faster, because you capture the product rather than produce video. Async video with committee tracking usually takes longer to stand up.


### Can either replace live demos?


For discovery, validation, and reach, yes: both let prospects self-serve without a rep, the exact bottleneck buyers describe. For complex negotiations, they augment live demos rather than replacing them.


### Do teams run both?


Rarely. Budget pressure pushes most teams to fund a single demo platform, so the practical decision is which one. Running both only makes sense when async video and interactive self-serve are genuinely separate jobs with separate budget.


### Which is better for enterprise?


It depends on motion, not size. Enterprises selling into large committees often value Consensus's video distribution and stakeholder analytics, while those running hands-on evaluations favor interactive tours from Walnut or Storylane.
